For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

content.content:
1	# wal-store
2	
3	Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.
4	
5	## Requirements
6	
7	Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.
8	
9	## Install
10	
11	    python3 -m pip install -e .
12	
13	## Run
14	
15	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
16	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
17	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>
18	
19	## Public interface
20	
21	`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
22	exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
23	line subcommand creates it).
24	- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
25	- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
26	- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
27	- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
28	  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
29	  the same call).
30	- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
31	  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
32	  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
33	  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
34	- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
35	- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
36	  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
37	  durable sequence.
38	- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
39	  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
40	- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
41	  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
42	  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
43	- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.
44	
45	## Scanning
46	
47	`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
48	returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
49	order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
50	exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
51	inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
52	unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
53	delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
54	only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
55	writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
56	invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
57	committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.
58	
59	The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
60	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
61	change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
62	sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
63	takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
64	of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
65	as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
66	context manager).
67	
68	## Resumable scans
69	
70	A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
71	the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
72	point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
73	token:
74	
75	- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
76	- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
77	  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
78	  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
79	  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.
80	
81	Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
82	the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
83	the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.
84	
85	The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
86	content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
87	scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
88	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
89	writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
90	immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
91	never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
92	log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
93	be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
94	read-only store never creates or modifies a file, even when minting a
95	token; such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
96	reconstruct) that snapshot.
97	
98	Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
99	resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
100	later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
101	neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
102	snapshot after the delete never shows the key.
103	
104	A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
105	corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
106	reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
107	foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
108	`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
109	`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
110	coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
111	the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
112	(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
113	be handed across platforms and processes.
114	
115	
116	## Historical snapshot lifecycle
117	
118	Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
119	without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
120	minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
121	every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
122	so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):
123	
124	- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
125	  one merely iterating, with no token minted) or any live read-only store
126	  is serving that snapshot. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
127	  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
128	  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
129	  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
130	  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
131	- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
132	  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
133	- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
134	  are deleted.
135	
136	A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
137	keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
138	committed log prefix or the checkpoint. Only once every copy is gone and
139	neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can rebuild the
140	snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
141	truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
142	`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.
143	
144	Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
145	a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
146	next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete an
147	in-use copy, cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state,
148	and never touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only
149	dead `wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies. It adds no command-line subcommand and no
150	new files: everything lives in the same store directory behind the
151	existing `scan`/token calls.
152	
153	
154	## Range deletes
155	
156	`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
157	of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
158	bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
159	`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
160	the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
161	shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
162	removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
163	endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
164	`ValueError`.
165	
166	Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
167	it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
168	writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
169	committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
170	alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
171	back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
172	new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
173	with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.
174	
175	Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
176	report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
177	it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
178	contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
179	reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
180	scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.
181	
182	## Read-only stores
183	
184	`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
185	number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
186	same directory. A reader takes no lock and never creates or changes a
187	file; it pins a snapshot at open time and every `get` reads from that one
188	complete committed snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written
189	commit, a torn record or a half-finished shrink are never visible.
190	Successive reads from the same reader may advance across snapshots only by

# wal-store

Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.

## Install

    python3 -m pip install -e .

## Run

    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>

## Public interface

`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
line subcommand creates it).
- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
  the same call).
- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
  durable sequence.
- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.

## Scanning

`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.

The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
context manager).

## Resumable scans

A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
token:

- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.

Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.

The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
read-only store never creates or modifies a file, even when minting a
token; such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
reconstruct) that snapshot.

Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
snapshot after the delete never shows the key.

A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
be handed across platforms and processes.


## Historical snapshot lifecycle

Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):

- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
  one merely iterating, with no token minted) or any live read-only store
  is serving that snapshot. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
  are deleted.

A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
committed log prefix or the checkpoint. Only once every copy is gone and
neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can rebuild the
snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.

Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete an
in-use copy, cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state,
and never touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only
dead `wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies. It adds no command-line subcommand and no
new files: everything lives in the same store directory behind the
existing `scan`/token calls.


## Range deletes

`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
`ValueError`.

Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.

Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.

## Read-only stores

`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
same directory. A reader takes no lock and never creates or changes a
file; it pins a snapshot at open time and every `get` reads from that one
complete committed snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written
commit, a torn record or a half-finished shrink are never visible.
Successive reads from the same reader may advance across snapshots only by
reopening; each read is of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not
replay the log and do not block the writer: killing or suspending a reader
never affects the writer's commits, recovery or stats. `put`, `delete`,
`commit` and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports
the pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.

`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.

## Recovery

`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:

- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final

Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,

The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with

110	create or modify a file. At open each one picks the highest committed prefix
111	available at that instant -- the validated ``wal.log`` prefix or ``wal.ckp``
112	-- scans it once into memory and serves every ``get`` from that index.
113	Because the chosen image is complete and is only ever replaced atomically
114	(never edited in place), a refresh caught mid-rename, a half-written commit,
115	a torn record, or a log being rebuilt, shrunk or compacted can never expose
116	partial bytes: each read lands on one full committed snapshot that was
117	current at or after the open. A directory written by an older version is
118	opened the same way from its log and checkpoint. Reads never replay the log
119	afterwards, so their cost is independent of history and they never block
120	the writer; a reader that is killed or simply hangs changes nothing on disk.
121	
122	Compaction (``Store.compact()``) rewrites the committed history into one
123	tight image without losing a byte of committed state. The compacted log
124	holds exactly the live puts -- one per currently committed key, in sorted
125	key order -- followed by a *base commit* marker carrying the pre-compaction
126	sequence number. The durable sequence keeps that value, so the next commit
127	is ``seq + 1`` and every later commit continues the strict sequence; keys
128	that were deleted never come back. The image is assembled in memory and
129	staged as the atomically replaced ``wal.cmp`` sidecar; finishing installs
130	it as ``wal.ckp`` first and as ``wal.log`` second. Every intermediate state
131	is therefore either the pair of old files or the pair of complete new
132	images, which is precisely the two-image world the reader already chooses
133	between: a kill anywhere leaves a state reopening converges by simply
134	repeating the finish, and interrupting compaction any number of times
135	produces the same bytes as one clean run. Live readers keep serving their
136	pinned old snapshots (the inode survives on Unix; on Windows readers hold
137	no writer-side fd) and new readers land on the new snapshot, never a mix,
138	a half-written file or a byte that was already reclaimed.
139	
140	The durable commit boundary is the highest of the validated log boundary,
141	the checkpoint boundary and the marker boundary, so it can never move
142	backwards. Every repair step is either idempotent or an atomic rename; a
143	kill between any two steps leaves a state the next open converges from to
144	the identical result.
145	
146	Log frame layout (all integers big-endian)::
147	
148	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
149	    | b"WAL2" | payload_length | header_crc | payload              | crc32   |
150	    | 4 bytes | 8 bytes        | 4 bytes    | metadata\\n<value>    | 4 bytes |
151	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
152	
153	``header_crc`` is the crc32 of the magic and length bytes. It makes a
154	partial header that borrows bytes from a following frame fail validation,
155	so an incomplete record in the middle of the log reads as corruption while
156	a genuinely short final header reads as a torn tail.
157	
158	Metadata is a compact JSON object: ``{"t":"p","k":key}`` for puts,
159	``{"t":"d","k":key}`` for deletes, ``{"t":"r","s":start,"e":end}`` for
160	range tombstones (``null`` marks an unbounded side), ``{"t":"c","s":seq}``
161	for ordinary commits and ``{"t":"b","s":seq}`` for the base commit that
162	closes a compacted log. The two carry the sequence identically; a base
163	marker is additionally required to be the first commit marker in its file.
164	The raw value bytes follow the first newline, so values need no encoding.
165	
166	A range tombstone covers every committed key whose raw UTF-8 bytes sort at
167	or after its start and strictly before its end (half-open). It is resolved
168	when the log is replayed -- matching keys are popped then -- and, like an
169	ordinary delete frame, carries no state of its own. Compaction therefore
170	reclaims it together with every other dead record: the live puts the
171	compact image contains already exclude each deleted key, so dropping the
172	tombstone can never make one reappear.
173	"""

189	class CorruptLogError(ValueError):
190	    """The write-ahead log is corrupt, not merely missing a torn tail.
191	
192	    A single incomplete final record is a normal crash remnant and is
193	    discarded during recovery. Anything else that fails framing, checksum,
194	    metadata or commit-sequence validation is corruption; recovery stops
195	    without applying or removing anything.
196	    """

199	class ScanCursor:
200	    """Ordered read-only cursor over one pinned committed snapshot.
201	
202	    Created by :meth:`Store.scan`. Iterating yields ``(key, value)`` pairs
203	    in bytewise key order -- keys ordered by their raw UTF-8 bytes, values
204	    returned as the exact stored bytes -- covering the range given at open:
205	    the start key inclusive, the end key exclusive, either side unbounded
206	    when its endpoint was ``None``.
207	
208	    The snapshot is fully materialised when the cursor opens, so later
209	    commits, compaction, crash recovery or reclamation of the old log space
210	    never change what the cursor yields, and closing the store it came from
211	    does not disturb it. The cursor is an iterator; it is also a context
212	    manager, and ``close()`` releases the snapshot early. Reading from a
213	    closed cursor raises ``ValueError``.
214	
215	    :meth:`token` serialises the current position into an opaque ``bytes``
216	    token naming the pinned snapshot, the scan range and the next position.
217	    ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this process or in a freshly opened
218	    store -- continues the identical scan from that position.
219	    """
220	
221	    def __init__(self, items, lo_idx=0, hi_idx=None, pos=None, seq=0,
222	                 lo=None, hi=None, publisher=None, sid=None):
223	        # ``items`` is the materialised snapshot: (key, value) pairs already
224	        # sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The visible window is
225	        # [lo_idx, hi_idx) and the next position starts at ``pos``.
226	        self._items = items
227	        self._lo_idx = lo_idx
228	        self._hi_idx = len(items) if hi_idx is None else hi_idx
229	        self._pos = lo_idx if pos is None else pos
230	        self._seq = seq
231	        self._lo = lo
232	        self._hi = hi
233	        # Writer-only callback durably publishing the pinned snapshot so a
234	        # minted token survives compaction and reclamation; ``None`` on
235	        # read-only stores, which never create or modify any file.
236	        self._publisher = publisher
237	        self._sid = sid
238	        # An open cursor counts as a user of its snapshot for the
239	        # reclamation rules: its box keeps the snapshot's pin alive in the
240	        # process-wide pin set until ``close()`` (or destruction), so
241	        # reclamation never removes the copy an open cursor is over. The
242	        # content identity is derived lazily on the first token mint.
243	        self._box = _register_snapshot(seq, items, sid)
244	        self._closed = False
245	
246	    def __iter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
247	        return self
248	
249	    def __next__(self):
250	        if self._closed:
251	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
252	        if self._pos >= self._hi_idx:
253	            raise StopIteration
254	        item = self._items[self._pos]
255	        self._pos += 1
256	        return item
257	
258	    def token(self) -> bytes:
259	        """Serialise the current position into an opaque scan token.
260	
261	        The returned ``bytes`` name the pinned snapshot (its durable
262	        sequence number and content identity), the scan range and the next
263	        position. Feeding the token to ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this
264	        process or in a freshly opened store, writer or read-only -- opens
265	        a cursor that continues the same range from the same position over
266	        the same pinned snapshot, byte-identical to the tail of this scan.
267	
268	        Token bytes are platform-independent and deterministic: the same
269	        snapshot at the same position always mints the same token. On a
270	        writer store minting also publishes the pinned snapshot as an
271	        immutable sidecar so the token survives compaction and reclamation
272	        of the old log space; a read-only store never writes anything.
273	        """
274	        if self._closed:
275	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
276	        if self._sid is None:
277	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self._items)
278	            # Share the derived identity with the pin box so the in-use
279	            # check at reclamation never hashes this snapshot again.
280	            self._box._sid = self._sid
281	        if self._publisher is not None:
282	            self._publisher(self._seq, self._sid, self._items)
283	        return _encode_token(self._seq, self._sid, self._lo, self._hi,
284	                             self._pos)
285	
286	    def mark(self) -> bytes:
287	        """Alias for :meth:`token`."""
288	        return self.token()
289	
290	    @property
291	    def closed(self) -> bool:
292	        return self._closed
293	
294	    def close(self) -> None:
295	        if self._closed:
296	            return
297	        _unpin_snapshot(self._box)
298	        self._items = []
299	        self._box = None
300	        self._closed = True
301	
302	    def __enter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
303	        return self
304	
305	    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> None:
306	        self.close()

330	# durable sequence, its 32-byte content identity, the optional range

342	def _snapshot_image(items) -> bytes:
343	    """Canonical byte image of a committed snapshot: one put frame per key.
344	
345	    ``items`` must already be sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The
346	    image uses the same deterministic framing as the log, so it is
347	    identical on every platform for the same snapshot.
348	    """
349	    return b"".join(_encode_frame(_OP_PUT, value, key=key)
350	                    for key, value in items)

353	def _snapshot_id(items) -> bytes:
354	    """Content identity of a committed snapshot (32 raw bytes)."""
355	    return hashlib.sha256(_snapshot_image(items)).digest()

358	def _encode_token(seq: int, sid: bytes, lo: bytes | None,
359	                  hi: bytes | None, pos: int) -> bytes:
360	    """Serialise a scan position; the exact inverse of :func:`_decode_token`."""
361	    flags = (1 if lo is not None else 0) | (2 if hi is not None else 0)
362	    parts = [_TOKEN_MAGIC, seq.to_bytes(8, "big"), sid, bytes((flags,))]
363	    for bound in (lo, hi):
364	        raw = bound if bound is not None else b""
365	        parts.append(len(raw).to_bytes(4, "big"))
366	        parts.append(raw)
367	    parts.append(pos.to_bytes(8, "big"))
368	    body = b"".join(parts)
369	    return body + zlib.crc32(body).to_bytes(4, "big")

372	def _decode_token(tok: bytes):
373	    """Parse a scan token into ``(seq, sid, lo, hi, pos)``.
374	
375	    Every malformation -- wrong magic, truncation, trailing garbage, a
376	    checksum mismatch, unknown flags, a hidden endpoint or a reversed
377	    range -- raises ``ValueError``; nothing is guessed or repaired.
378	    """
379	    if len(tok) < 4 + 8 + 32 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 4:
380	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
381	    if tok[:4] != _TOKEN_MAGIC:
382	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
383	    if int.from_bytes(tok[-4:], "big") != zlib.crc32(tok[:-4]):
384	        raise ValueError("scan token checksum mismatch")
385	    off = 4
386	    seq = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
387	    off += 8
388	    sid = tok[off:off + 32]
389	    off += 32
390	    flags = tok[off]
391	    off += 1
392	    if flags & ~0x03:
393	        raise ValueError("scan token carries unknown flags")
394	    bounds = []
395	    for present in (flags & 1, flags & 2):
396	        if off + 4 > len(tok) - 4:
397	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
398	        size = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 4], "big")
399	        off += 4
400	        if off + size > len(tok) - 4:
401	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
402	        if not present and size != 0:
403	            raise ValueError("scan token carries a hidden endpoint")
404	        bounds.append(tok[off:off + size] if present else None)
405	        off += size
406	    if off + 8 != len(tok) - 4:
407	        raise ValueError("scan token length mismatch")
408	    pos = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
409	    lo, hi = bounds
410	    if lo is not None and hi is not None and lo > hi:
411	        raise ValueError("scan token range is reversed")
412	    return seq, sid, lo, hi, pos

415	class _SnapshotBox:
416	    """Strong box around one user's materialised, pinned snapshot.
417	
418	    A box is the unit the reclamation logic counts as a user: every open
419	    cursor and every read-only store holds its own box for the snapshot it
420	    serves. Boxes live in a process-wide :class:`weakref.WeakSet`, so a
421	    cursor or reader that is garbage collected without an explicit
422	    ``close()`` releases its pin automatically -- the in-use table can
423	    neither leak nor outlive the snapshots it protects. The content
424	    identity is hashed lazily, so merely opening a scan that never mints a
425	    token pays no hashing cost.
426	    """
427	
428	    __slots__ = ("seq", "items", "_sid", "__weakref__")
429	
430	    def __init__(self, seq, items, sid=None):
431	        self.seq = seq
432	        self.items = items
433	        self._sid = sid
434	
435	    def sid(self) -> bytes:
436	        if self._sid is None:
437	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self.items)
438	        return self._sid

441	# Process-wide set of snapshots currently in use. Every open cursor and
442	# every live read-only store keeps a box here for its pinned snapshot; the
443	# writer's reclamation never removes the published copy of any snapshot
444	# named in this set. The set is weak, so users closed normally (or simply
445	# dropped) release their pin with no bookkeeping. The boxes also keep the
446	# materialised bytes alive in memory, so a token minted in this process
447	# resolves without touching disk even across stores.
448	_PINS: "weakref.WeakSet" = weakref.WeakSet()
449	
450	
451	def _register_snapshot(seq: int, items, sid=None) -> _SnapshotBox:
452	    """Register one user (a cursor or a reader) pinning a snapshot."""
453	    box = _SnapshotBox(seq, items, sid)
454	    _PINS.add(box)
455	    return box
456	
457	
458	def _unpin_snapshot(box: _SnapshotBox) -> None:
459	    """Release the pin held by a closing cursor or reader."""
460	    _PINS.discard(box)
461	
462	
463	def _live_snapshot_keys() -> set:
464	    """The ``(seq, sid)`` pairs with at least one user in this process."""
465	    return {(box.seq, box.sid()) for box in _PINS}

468	def _pinned_snapshot(seq: int, sid: bytes):
469	    """Materialised items for a live in-process pin, or ``None``.
470	
471	    The identity is compared only for boxes already on the token's
472	    sequence, so a resolution against an unpinned sequence hashes nothing.
473	    """
474	    for box in _PINS:
475	        if box.seq == seq and box.sid() == sid:
476	            return box.items
477	    return None

486	def _range_bounds_from_meta(meta) -> tuple[bytes | None, bytes | None]:
487	    """Decode and validate the two endpoints of a range tombstone frame.
488	
489	    Returns their raw UTF-8 bytes, ``None`` for a ``null`` (unbounded)
490	    side. Missing, mistyped or unencodable endpoints are corruption.
491	    """
492	    if not isinstance(meta, dict):
493	        raise CorruptLogError(f"invalid range tombstone metadata: {meta!r}")
494	    if "s" not in meta or "e" not in meta:
495	        raise CorruptLogError(
496	            f"range tombstone is missing an endpoint: {meta!r}")
497	    lo = meta.get("s")
498	    hi = meta.get("e")
499	    for endpoint in (lo, hi):
500	        if endpoint is not None and not isinstance(endpoint, str):
501	            raise CorruptLogError(
502	                f"invalid range tombstone endpoint: {meta!r}")
503	    try:
504	        lo_b = lo.encode("utf-8") if lo is not None else None
505	        hi_b = hi.encode("utf-8") if hi is not None else None
506	    except (UnicodeEncodeError, AttributeError):
507	        raise CorruptLogError(
508	            f"invalid range tombstone endpoint: {meta!r}")
509	    return lo_b, hi_b

512	def _key_in_range(key_bytes: bytes, lo: bytes | None,
513	                  hi: bytes | None) -> bool:
514	    """Half-open bytewise membership: ``lo <= key < hi``, null unbounded."""
515	    if lo is not None and key_bytes < lo:
516	        return False
517	    if hi is not None and key_bytes >= hi:
518	        return False
519	    return True

522	def _encode_frame(op: str, value: bytes = b"", key: str | None = None,
523	                  seq: int | None = None, start: str | None = None,
524	                  end: str | None = None) -> bytes:
525	    meta: dict[str, object] = {"t": op}
526	    if op == _OP_RANGE:
527	        # Both endpoints are always carried; null leaves that side open.
528	        meta["s"] = start
529	        meta["e"] = end
530	    else:
531	        if key is not None:
532	            meta["k"] = key
533	        if seq is not None:
534	            meta["s"] = seq
535	    head = json.dumps(meta, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
536	    payload = head + b"\n" + value
537	    prefix = _MAGIC + len(payload).to_bytes(8, "big")
538	    header = prefix + zlib.crc32(prefix).to_bytes(4, "big")
539	    return header + payload + zlib.crc32(payload).to_bytes(4, "big")

542	def _iter_frames(f):
543	    """Scan an open binary log file from position 0.
544	
545	    For every intact frame yields
546	    ``("frame", meta, value, start, end)``. Scanning stops with either no
547	    terminal event (clean EOF), ``("torn", start)`` for a single incomplete
548	    final frame, or ``("invalid", start)`` for a frame that fails framing,
549	    header/payload checksum or metadata parsing. With the header checksum a
550	    partial header that borrows bytes from a following record cannot survive,
551	    so a short read landing exactly at EOF is reliably the one unfinished
552	    record a single writer was appending when it died; bytes left beyond such
553	    a read instead make it corruption.
554	    """
555	    f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
556	    eof = f.tell()
557	    f.seek(0)
558	    while True:
559	        start = f.tell()
560	        header = f.read(_HEADER)
561	        if not header:
562	            return
563	        if len(header) < _HEADER:
564	            # Trailing bytes of a frame header are a torn tail only when
565	            # nothing follows them; a gap anywhere else is corruption.
566	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
567	                   else ("invalid", start))
568	            return
569	        if header[:4] != _MAGIC:
570	            yield "invalid", start
571	            return
572	        if int.from_bytes(header[_PREFIX:], "big") != zlib.crc32(
573	                header[:_PREFIX]):
574	            yield "invalid", start
575	            return
576	        length = int.from_bytes(header[4:_PREFIX], "big")
577	        if length > _MAX_PAYLOAD:
578	            yield "invalid", start
579	            return
580	        payload = f.read(length)
581	        checksum = f.read(_TRAILER)
582	        if len(payload) < length or len(checksum) < _TRAILER:
583	            # Only the single final record may be incomplete.
584	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
585	                   else ("invalid", start))
586	            return
587	        if int.from_bytes(checksum, "big") != zlib.crc32(payload):
588	            yield "invalid", start
589	            return
590	        newline = payload.find(b"\n")
591	        if newline < 0:
592	            yield "invalid", start
593	            return
594	        try:
595	            meta = json.loads(payload[:newline])
596	        except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
597	            yield "invalid", start
598	            return
599	        if not isinstance(meta, dict) or not isinstance(meta.get("t"), str):
600	            yield "invalid", start
601	            return
602	        yield "frame", meta, payload[newline + 1:], start, f.tell()

605	def _fsync_dir(path: str) -> None:
606	    """Fsync a directory so a nearby rename/unlink is durable.
607	
608	    Windows cannot open directories for fsync and raises ``PermissionError``
609	    (access denied); directory entries there are made durable by the file's
610	    own flush-on-rename, so skipping the directory fsync keeps store creation
611	    working everywhere. Other platforms occasionally refuse the directory
612	    open or the fsync (restrictive mounts, virtualised FSes); that is
613	    likewise best-effort -- the file's own fsync is what carries the data.
614	    Any refusal, whatever ``OSError`` form it takes, is absorbed: a rejected
615	    directory sync never aborts store creation, a commit or a compaction,
616	    and never affects later writes.
617	    """
618	    if sys.platform == "win32":
619	        return
620	    try:
621	        fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)
622	    except OSError:
623	        return
624	    try:
625	        try:
626	            os.fsync(fd)
627	        except OSError:
628	            # Some non-Windows mounts reject directory fsync, in any form.
629	            pass
630	    finally:
631	        os.close(fd)

640	def inject_tear(source, destination, offset):
641	    """Copy a log cut at exactly ``offset`` bytes, for bytewise verification.
642	
643	    Produces ``destination`` containing the first ``offset`` bytes of
644	    ``source`` -- a replica of a process killed precisely when the write had
645	    reached that byte offset. The source file is never modified. Either path
646	    argument may be a store directory, in which case its ``wal.log`` is used.
647	
648	    ``offset`` must satisfy ``0 <= offset <= len(source)``; a negative or
649	    past-the-end offset raises ``IndexError``. The full-length copy
650	    (``offset == len(source)``) is the clean control case.
651	
652	    Verification aid only; the normal write path never calls this.
653	    """
654	    if not isinstance(offset, int) or isinstance(offset, bool):
655	        raise TypeError("offset must be an integer byte offset")
656	
657	    src = os.path.join(source, LOG_NAME) if os.path.isdir(source) else source
658	    dst = (os.path.join(destination, LOG_NAME)
659	           if os.path.isdir(destination) else destination)
660	
661	    size = os.path.getsize(src)
662	    if offset < 0 or offset > size:
663	        raise IndexError(
664	            f"tear offset {offset} out of range for log of {size} bytes")
665	    if os.path.abspath(src) == os.path.abspath(dst):
666	        raise ValueError("tear destination must differ from the source log")
667	
668	    remaining = offset
669	    with open(src, "rb") as fsrc, open(dst, "wb") as fdst:
670	        while remaining:
671	            chunk = fsrc.read(min(remaining, 1 << 20))

681	class Store:

684	    ``path`` must be an existing store directory; the log file inside it is

691	    read-only processes may coexist with the one writer. The reader pins the
692	    committed snapshot current at open time -- the highest committed prefix

695	    snapshot is independent of the log's later history, so a read never
696	    replays the log and cannot block the writer, and uncommitted bytes, a

699	    ``delete_range``, ``commit``, ``recover`` and ``compact``

704	    :class:`ScanCursor` over the complete committed snapshot pinned at the

781	    @staticmethod
